scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that job prospects matter, then argues they should not be the sole basis for choosing a field; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Choosing what to study is one of the most important decisions a young person makes.
Some people claim that students should base this choice on the availability of jobs in each field.
I agree that job prospects deserve serious thought, but I do not believe they should be the only basis for the decision.
First, it is sensible for students to consider where the jobs are.
A degree that leads to steady work offers security and the freedom that a reliable income brings.
For example, a student who trains in nursing or engineering can usually expect dependable employment after graduating.
This shows that practical concerns are not selfish but a reasonable part of planning a life.
Ignoring the job market entirely can leave a graduate with heavy debt and few options.
Knowing that a field offers opportunities can also reduce stress and uncertainty.
To this extent, the claim gives useful advice.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why it should not be the only basis

sentences.text: Second, however, choosing a field by jobs alone can lead to an unhappy and unproductive life.
People rarely do well at work they find dull or meaningless, however secure it may be.
Consider a talented artist who forces herself into accounting only because it pays, then performs poorly and soon quits.
This kind of mismatch wastes both her talent and the years she spent training.
Job markets also change quickly, so today's safe choice may not be safe in ten years.
Genuine interest, by contrast, tends to produce the energy and skill that lead to success.
A good decision therefore weighs passion and ability alongside job prospects.
In conclusion, the availability of jobs is an important factor that students should not ignore.
But basing the choice on jobs alone risks a career without interest or strength.
The wisest students choose a field where their interests and their prospects meet.
